title: A packaged food is many chains meeting

blocks.html: Checked against the sources as they stood on 2026-09-25.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A packaged food made from several ingredients is where several supply chains meet.

The Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020, made by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), govern what the label of a pre-packaged food must declare. Regulation 5(2)(b) requires the ingredients to be “listed in descending order of their composition by weight or volume, as the case may be at the time of its manufacture”. The list therefore ranks the ingredients. It states an ingredient’s percentage only where regulation 5(2)(g) requires one: where the label emphasises that ingredient in words or pictures, or where the ingredient characterises the food and leaving its percentage out would mislead.

Some ingredients may be declared under a class title. Sucrose may be declared as “Sugar”, and glucose as “Dextrose or Glucose”. Milk products may be declared as “Milk solids”; the label may also say where the solids came from, but need not. Spices, herbs and condiments may be declared together under one class title. An edible vegetable oil must be declared by the name of the specific oil.

The label must name the brand owner, who may be the manufacturer or only the marketer (regulation 5(6)). It must also show the brand owner’s licence number, the number of the licence a food business holds under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (regulation 5(7)). If the manufacturer is someone else, its licence number must also appear; its name need not (regulation 5(7)(b)). A country of origin is required for food imported into India (regulation 5(12)).

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Turn over a packet of biscuits. The list of ingredients on the back is a map of farms.

Wheat flour came from wheat fields. Sugar came from a sugar crop and a sugar mill. Milk solids came from dairy animals. Then the packets travelled another chain to your shop.

The ingredients go in order of weight when the food was made, heaviest first (by volume for some liquid foods). So the first ingredient weighs more than any other single one.

The label also leaves a great deal out.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Here is the trap with the address on a food packet. It looks like the place the food comes from. It is not.

Pick up any packet of biscuits and find the words “Manufactured by” or “Marketed by”. Read the address under them.

Now open the Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020, in FSSAI’s compendium at https://www.fssai.gov.in/upload/uploadfiles/files/Comp_Labelling%20Display_Version%20VIII_09_09_2025.pdf and search inside it for “brand owner”.

The name and complete address of the brand owner, whether or not, he himself is the manufacturer, marketer, packer or bottler, as the case may be, shall be declared on the label.

So the address is the brand owner’s. If your packet says “Marketed by”, the company named there may never have baked a biscuit. Read on to regulation 5(7)(b). When the maker is someone else, the label must show the maker’s licence number; it need not show its name. That number may be your only lead to the factory.

And nothing on the label leads past the factory. The address is not the mill that ground the flour, and not the farm that grew the wheat. The label tells you who answers for the packet. It does not tell you where the food came from.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: Some packets are made by the brand owner itself, and then the address is the maker’s. Food imported into India must also name its country of origin and its importer. The trap is assuming the address is the source without checking which of these cases you hold.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Now read the list of ingredients as a map. The list below is made up, not copied from any real brand. It is written the way regulation 5(2) requires: “Ingredients: Wheat flour (Atta), Sugar, Edible vegetable oil (Palm oil), Dextrose, Milk solids, Choco chips, Iodised salt.”

Two kinds of name on it need a word. “Sugar” is a class title — one name the regulation allows for a whole group of ingredients. “Dextrose” is another; it stands for glucose, which the regulation counts among sugars. “Choco chips” is a compound ingredient — one that is itself made of two or more ingredients.

Take the ingredients one at a time. For each, write the crop behind it and the chain it came up. The table is a sketch: the right-hand column is what you would still have to find out.

On the list What the regulation lets it say Where it starts The chain before the factory What the label does not tell you
Wheat flour (Atta) the ingredient’s own name wheat farm, trader, flour mill which state, which mill
Sugar “Sugar” may stand for sucrose a sugar crop farm, sugar mill which crop, which mill
Edible vegetable oil (Palm oil) the specific oil must be named oil palm plantation, oil mill, refinery which country
Dextrose “Dextrose” may stand for glucose a crop the label does not name farm, processor which crop
Milk solids “Milk solids” may stand for any milk product milk dairy farm, dairy plant which dairy, which animal
Choco chips a compound ingredient, named as such several several its own ingredients, if under 5 per cent
Iodised salt the ingredient’s own name salt wherever the salt is made where

Now test what the order can tell you. Wheat flour comes first, so it weighed more than the sugar at manufacture. But sugar appears twice, as “Sugar” and as “Dextrose”. The rule ranks each named ingredient on its own. Added together, the two sweeteners might outweigh the flour, or might not. The list cannot say.

Last, look at “Choco chips”. If they make up less than 5 per cent of the biscuit, the regulation does not require their own ingredients to be listed, apart from additives. Their sugar, fat and cocoa each came up a chain too. On this label, those chains are out of sight.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: The order is fixed at manufacture, by weight or by volume. It ranks ingredients and gives no amounts, unless regulation 5(2)(g) requires a percentage, as it does for an ingredient the label emphasises. A single-ingredient food, such as a packet of plain atta, needs no list at all. And a map drawn from the list stops at the factory door: which farms, mills and countries sit behind each line is for other sources to answer.

points.html: “The first ingredient is most of the product” is wrong. The first is only heavier than each other single ingredient.

Add up an ingredient that appears under more than one name before you say where it ranks. Sugar and dextrose are listed as two lines, each in its own place. Together they may outrank the first ingredient.
The address on a packet is the brand owner’s, who may only market it. If the maker is someone else, the label must show the maker’s licence number; it need not show its name.

A compound ingredient (regulation 5(2)(e)) under 5 per cent of the food need not list its own ingredients, apart from additives. When you trace a product’s chains, mark such an ingredient as a known gap, not as one chain.
The label asks for a country of origin only on food imported into India. Do not read silence on the label as evidence that an ingredient is Indian.
For any packaged food, read the first four or five ingredients as a list of farm chains.
The list is one pack’s ranking at manufacture, under one set of rules. It cannot tell you who supplied an ingredient, what it cost, or who kept how much of the price.

blocks.prompt: A made-up packet of namkeen lists: “Ingredients: Gram pulse flour (Besan), Edible vegetable oil (Palmolein), Peanuts, Iodised salt, Spices and condiments.” Name the chain behind each ingredient. Which ingredient hides more than one chain behind a single name, and which rule lets it?
blocks.answer:
Besan starts with a pulse crop, gram, and goes through a farm, a trader and a mill. Palmolein starts with the oil palm and goes through a plantation, an oil mill and a refinery; the label does not say in which country. Peanuts start with the groundnut crop. Iodised salt starts wherever the salt is made.

“Spices and condiments” hides several chains. The class-title table in regulation 5(2)(d) lets all spices, herbs and condiments, and their extracts, be declared under one class title. So chilli, turmeric or cumin, each with its own farms, may sit behind those three words. The edible oil, by contrast, had to be named, which is why you know it is palmolein.

blocks.prompt: The front of a made-up packet says “Made with real milk” beside a picture of a glass of milk. The list shows “Milk solids” as the eighth ingredient, with no percentage. A friend says: “Eighth means there’s hardly any milk in it.” What can you say, and what should you look for?
blocks.answer:
Eighth means milk solids weighed less than each of seven other ingredients at manufacture. It does not say how little. Seven heavier ingredients could leave milk solids as a large share or a tiny one.

The front of the pack emphasises milk in words and a picture. Regulation 5(2)(g) requires the percentage of an ingredient emphasised that way, subject to listed exemptions. So look for a percentage beside milk solids. If none is there, the list is not answering the question your friend is asking. Whether the label complies is a question for FSSAI, not something the order can settle.

blocks.prompt: A health secretary asks why a packet of biscuits should concern anyone beyond the food regulator. Write the answer you would give, answer first, in no more than a page.
blocks.answer:
Because a packet of biscuits is several farm chains meeting in one factory.

The label regulation fixes only how the packet declares its ingredients. What goes into it, at what price, was decided further back. Wheat, sugar, edible oil and milk each came through farmers, traders and mills before the factory bought them. A change in any one of those chains reaches the biscuit through the factory’s buying.

So a question about what is in the packet is also a question about farms, mills and trade. The label is where you start reading, not where the answer is.
